headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress make LangGraph→Open Interpreter pair dangerous by default; prompt injection and cascading errors are also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can pass application-defined files and stdout/stderr between nodes, while Open Interpreter reads the local filesystem and clipboard by default. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if LangGraph outputs are fed into Open Interpreter without sanitization. The pair is not provably isolated, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF LangGraph writes attacker-controlled text into a file or stdout that Open Interpreter later ingests as instructions
IF the orchestrator copies LangGraph output into Open Interpreter via clipboard or shared files
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of prior-agent output
Use a strict prompt/template wrapper for any handoff text
Store handoff artifacts in a read-only directory
Require human review before Open Interpreter executes generated code
requires-engineering: add provenance tags and content filtering between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph can touch graph state and broad network egress, while Open Interpreter can access the entire user filesystem and also egress broadly. If both run on the same machine or workspace, sensitive local files can flow into model-provider APIs through Open Interpreter, and LangGraph state can also be exposed through shared files. The default blast radius includes secrets and local data, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents share a local workspace or filesystem
IF Open Interpreter is allowed to read files that contain secrets or sensitive documents
IF either agent forwards file contents to a model provider or external API
mitigations: Restrict both agents to separate directories
Remove sensitive files from the shared machine before running
Disable network egress for one or both agents during sensitive tasks
Use a dedicated low-privilege OS account for Open Interpreter
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention and egress allowlists

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have write_filesystem and execute_shell, and Open Interpreter also modify_git_state plus filesystem-wide access. LangGraph can orchestrate multiple nodes with shared state via a checkpointer, while Open Interpreter shares state via filesystem. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can corrupt files or git state without locking, so the conflict is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git repository
IF LangGraph nodes and Open Interpreter run concurrently without external locking
IF Open Interpreter is permitted to commit or rewrite files while LangGraph is active
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate working tree
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Avoid git operations from Open Interpreter during paired runs
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control and transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a low-level orchestrator that can emit structured outputs from one node to another, and Open Interpreter can execute shell commands and browser actions from those inputs. If LangGraph-produced facts or instructions are treated as authoritative, Open Interpreter may act on them without verification, creating a strong cascading-error pathway. The downstream action authority makes high appropriate.
conditions: IF LangGraph output is passed directly into Open Interpreter as task text or code
IF Open Interpreter executes commands without a separate verification step
IF the workflow allows browser or shell actions based on untrusted upstream output
mitigations: Insert a verification step before execution
Require explicit human approval for generated commands
Constrain Open Interpreter to dry-run mode for handoffs
Log and diff all upstream outputs before actioning them
requires-engineering: add schema validation and policy checks between agents

E_compliance.rationale: LangGraph touches application-defined graph state, while Open Interpreter can access anything reachable on the local machine and the entire user filesystem. If regulated data such as EU PII or secrets are present locally, Open Interpreter may process them under a different retention or residency regime than the application state managed by LangGraph. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored on the local machine accessible to Open Interpreter
IF the application state managed by LangGraph has stricter retention or residency rules than the local filesystem
IF Open Interpreter sends locally stored regulated data to a third-party model provider
mitigations: Keep regulated data off the shared machine
Separate retention policies for app state and local files
Disable Open Interpreter on datasets with residency constraints
Review logging settings before each run
requires-engineering: implement residency-aware routing and retention enforcement
